Trump administration sued over fatal Minneapolis shooting
The family of Renee Good, one of two U.S. citizens fatally shot by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis in January, sued the Trump administration on Thursday, saying there had been “no accountability” for her killing during deportation sweeps.
Good, 37, was shot dead in her car by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent on Jan. 7 when she and her wife joined one of the city’s daily protests against masked and armed federal agents deployed to Minnesota to arrest migrants for deportation.
The two lawsuits accuse Jonathan Ross, the ICE agent who shot Good, and senior Trump administration officials of unconstitutional negligence and excessive force that violated the civil rights of Good and others in Minneapolis, demanding a jury trial and damages. They are among the first major civil actions taken against US President Donald Trump for his unprecedented deportation sweeps in Minneapolis last winter, dubbed Operation Metro Surge.
“What happened to Renee was completely senseless and the fact that there’s been no accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy is completely mind-blowing,” Brett Ganger, Good’s brother, said at a press conference in Minneapolis. “What happened to America? Something must change now.”
Ross could not be reached for comment on Thursday, while a White House spokeswoman called the lawsuits baseless.
Good’s killing intensified the backlash in Minnesota and beyond against the sweeps, involving thousands of immigration agents deployed to street patrols in Minnesota. Trump ended the Minnesota surge in February, but says his anti-immigration policies are needed for the safety of native-born Americans.

Days after Good’s death, an ICE agent shot and wounded Julio Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan delivery driver, in the leg, and two weeks later when immigration agents fatally shot Alex Pretti, an American nurse working for the US Department of Veterans Affairs.
Senior Trump administration officials initially branded Good a “domestic terrorist” and the Department of Justice stopped its federal prosecutors in Minneapolis from investigating the agents involved in her killing, prompting at least half a dozen of those prosecutors to resign in protest. None of the agents involved has yet faced any charges.
The lawsuits describe Good as a poet and mother of three children, and that she and her wife, Becca Good, dropped their 6-year-old son off at school before stopping her car in the middle of Portland Avenue after seeing patrolling ICE agents.
“Renee honked her horn to warn her neighbors,” according to the lawsuits. “Her partner got out and began to film. Renee stayed behind the wheel. She was not the target of any investigation, and she was breaking no law that any federal officer had authority to enforce.”
Becca Good, in her first public remarks, said of her wife: “She was pure love. She was funny. She was smart. She was gorgeous.”
“Renee believed in something simple: that being good can change the world,” she said. “She believed everyone deserves love and compassion, care and dignity, no matter who they were or where they came from.”
Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said the administration would “vigorously defend” itself against the lawsuits.
“The Trump administration views the deaths of countless innocent Americans at the hands of criminal illegal aliens as a tragedy that should warrant equal coverage from the mainstream media who choose to ignore these victims of illegal alien crime,” she said in a statement.
‘I’m not mad at you’
Good’s killing was captured on widely viewed videos that showed Ross approaching Good in her car partly blocking the road moments after he had driven past her. Ross circled her car on foot, recording on his cellphone.
In her last words, Good can be seen on video saying to Ross: “That’s fine, dude, I’m not mad at you.”
Moments later, another ICE agent approached the car and told Good to get out. She can be seen reversing briefly, then putting the car into forward gear and turning the steering wheel to her right, apparently trying to drive away.
As the car moves forward, Ross, who at that point had returned to the front left of her car, shouts “Whoa!” and shoots into the car, hitting Good three times: in her head, arm and torso.
Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, the chief elected prosecutor in Minneapolis, is investigating the agents who killed Good and Pretti for possible violations of Minnesota law. The investigations have been slowed because the Justice Department withdrew its usual cooperation and evidence-sharing with local law enforcement agencies. Minnesota has sued the Trump administration to gain access to the evidence it gathered at the shooting scenes.
Ross has not publicly discussed Good’s death or his actions that day. The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE and related agencies, has defended the conduct of Ross and other immigration officers as justified uses of force in dangerous situations.

sources.news_title: Renee Good’s family sues US government and immigration officials over her killing in Minneapolis - The Boston Globe
sources.text:
Renee Good’s family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials Thursday, alleging wrongful death, conspiracy and other violations in the 37-year-old woman’s killing by an immigration officer during a federal crackdown in Minneapolis.
The two lawsuits were filed by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and Renee’s brother Brent Ganger.
“She was pure love. She was funny. She was smart,” Becca Good said during a news conference to announce the lawsuits. “She was the center of my universe.”
The Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to an email seeking comment.
Officer shot Good as she turned her car away from him
Renee Good was fatally shot Jan. 7 as protests against immigration raids flared across the city. According to Becca Good, her partner stopped their car in a street to support neighbors during an immigration operation.
Bystander video shows Renee Good in the driver’s seat of a red SUV blocking part of the road and repeatedly honking her horn.
Two immigration officers get out of a truck, their faces covered, and one orders Good to get out of the car. She reverses briefly, then turns the steering wheel as the officer says again, “get out of the car.”
Almost simultaneously, Becca Good, standing in the street, shouts: “Drive, baby, drive!”
One officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and fires into the windshield. He lurches back as the car turns away from him. The officer, who is now very close to the open window on the driver’s side, fires two more times, fatally shooting Renee Good, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.
Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense and that Good had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism.”
One lawsuit alleges wrongful death
The lawsuit against the United States of America seeks damages for Good’s wrongful death and “the immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family,” according to a news release by lawyers for Ganger and Good.
The lawsuit, which seeks a bench trial, also alleges “intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligent infliction of emotional distress” on Becca Good.
Becca and Renee Good, the mother of three children, were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives. They had only recently relocated to Minneapolis from Kansas City, Missouri.
Another lawsuit alleges conspiracy to conceal evidence
The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights and seeks a jury trial. It says the federal government moved to hide the evidence of what actually happened on Jan. 7.
The lawsuit says the shots fired by Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who killed Good, “were the predictable and intended product of the operation.”
It describes a “carefully planned, coordinated effort between senior federal officials and private actors to make two ethnic communities — Minnesotans of Somali and Hispanic descent and origin — the object of aggression and abduction, and to silence by intimidation, arrest and violence the neighbors and allies of those targeted communities who observed, documented and warned of that campaign.”
The lawsuit names Ross as a defendant, as well as: White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller; former Homeland Security head Kristi Noem; Corey Lewandowski, a campaign manager for President Donald Trump who also served as one of Noem’s advisers; White House border czar Tom Homan; former acting director of U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement Todd Lyons; former U.S. Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino; and 10 unnamed federal agents.
Good’s partner acknowledges other lives lost in immigration crackdown
The killing of Good and another U.S. citizen, Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis just weeks later sparked outrage across the country and calls to rein in immigration enforcement. At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration officers during President Donald Trump’s second term.
In social media accounts, Renee Good described herself as a “poet and writer and wife and mom.” On Pinterest, a profile picture shows her smiling and holding a young child, alongside posts about tattoos, hairstyles and home decorating.
In an interview shortly after her death, Renee Good’s mother, Donna Ganger, told The Associated Press: “She had this way of making you feel special and loved that I didn’t even understand that until we lost her.”
Good’s partner noted the broader loss to communities nationwide.
“As we have tried to navigate our own massive loss, I am also devastated by how many other lives have been destroyed in this darkest of times,” Becca Good said in the news release Thursday. “So many other families are dealing with the loss of their loved ones; to everyone who has had to witness it — the pain of this moment extends far beyond our family. What happened to us should never happen to any family.”
McCormack reported from Concord, New Hampshire.

The family of Renee Good filed two federal lawsuits seeking damages over her January shooting death, alleging an ICE officer used unjustified deadly force and that federal personnel violated her constitutional and civil rights.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
The family of Renee Good filed two lawsuits Thursday against the U.S. government and federal immigration personnel over her fatal shooting by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer in Minneapolis in January, alleging wrongful death, excessive force and violations of federal and Minnesota law.
Good was shot after an encounter with federal immigration officers while sitting in her vehicle with her wife, Becca Good, nearby. Federal officials previously defended the shooting as an act of self-defense, saying Good drove her vehicle toward an agent. Her family’s complaints present a sharply different account, alleging she was attempting to “drive slowly away” when the officer opened fire.
The lawsuits allege the officer violated Good’s Fourth Amendment protection against unreasonable searches and seizures and breached Department of Homeland Security use-of-force policies that permit deadly force only when an officer reasonably believes there is an imminent threat of death or serious bodily injury. The family also alleges battery, false imprisonment, negligence and intentional infliction of emotional distress.
According to the complaints, Good and her wife were in their neighborhood as federal officers carried out immigration enforcement operations. Good allegedly honked her horn to alert neighbors to the officers’ presence but had not committed or threatened violence before the confrontation.
Her attorneys argue that she had a constitutional right to observe federal law enforcement activity, express herself and leave the area.
“Renee told masked agents she wasn’t mad at them; her last words clearly reflected her state of mind. Renee had the right to speak, express herself, assemble, observe and leave the scene unharmed and alive,” said Antonio M. Romanucci, founding partner of Romanucci & Blandin and one of the attorneys representing the family.
“Today, these lawsuits are the beginning of the ultimate legal weapon in uncovering the truth behind this unlawful use of deadly force and the nefarious conspiracies behind the invasion of American cities by American law enforcement officers,” Romanucci added.
The complaints also accuse DHS personnel at the scene of unlawfully confining Good and causing emotional distress. Her family is seeking monetary damages, with one case requesting a bench trial and the other asking for a jury trial.
Good’s brother, Brett Ganger, said the litigation is intended to seek accountability on behalf of his sister and her children.
“I stand here with fierce determination to do what is right for my sister, for her children, and for our country—and that is to insist on accountability,” Ganger said.
Becca Good said the family wants the case to prevent another family from experiencing a similar loss.
“What happened to us should never happen to any family. No child should grow up without a parent because of it. No one should lose their sister or their daughter. No one should have to live without their soulmate. Accountability—real accountability—is the only way to make sure that no other family has to go through what we have,” she said.
The shooting became a major point of controversy surrounding federal immigration enforcement in Minnesota. Video from the encounter and conflicting interpretations of Good’s movements immediately before the gunfire fueled disagreement over whether the officer faced an imminent threat when he fired.
The family’s lawsuits will require a federal court to examine those circumstances more closely, including the officer’s actions, Good’s vehicle movement and whether federal personnel complied with constitutional standards and DHS policies governing deadly force.
The filings are civil complaints and do not establish wrongdoing. The federal government and individual defendants will have an opportunity to dispute the family’s allegations and present their own evidence and legal defenses.
The White House and DHS did not respond to requests for comment before publication. A Department of Justice spokesperson said the department does not comment on pending litigation or investigations.
Good’s family is now asking the federal court to determine whether her death resulted from lawful self-defense, as federal officials have maintained, or an unconstitutional use of deadly force, as the lawsuits allege.

sources.news_title: Renee Good’s Family Sues Trump Administration Months After ICE Agent Fatally Shot Her in Minneapolis
sources.text:
Renee Good’s family has filed two federal civil lawsuits alleging wrongful death and excessive force nine months after an immigration officer fatally shot the mom of three in Minneapolis.
According to court documents obtained by Us on Thursday, October 1, Good’s family claims ICE agents violated the Fourth Amendment and mandatory policies within the Department of Homeland Security.
“Renee was not the target of any law enforcement investigation. She had no criminal history,” the lawsuit alleges. “ICE agents are not empowered to enforce Minnesota traffic laws. No agent at the scene possessed any evidence or information that Renee had engaged in any unlawful obstructive conduct.”
The lawsuit seeks to hold the United States liable under the Federal Tort Claims Act for the actions of federal agents. It alleges wrongful death, battery, assault, false imprisonment, infliction of emotional distress and negligence.
Us has reached out to the White House for comment.
Good, 37, was fatally shot in the driver’s seat of her SUV during a January 7 encounter with ICE officer Jonathan Ross, where she and her partner had been joining one of the city’s daily protests.
The killing occurred about a month after President Donald Trump’s administration deployed 3,000 immigration agents to the Twin Cities of Minneapolis in what officials have dubbed Operation Metro Surge.
“I stand here with fierce determination to do what is right for my sister, for her children, and for our country — and that is to insist on accountability,” Good’s brother, Brent Ganger, said in a statement via NBC News. “What happened to her on January 7th and what has happened to far too many people in the last year is not what America is about. We can and must do better, and the Constitution must be the roadmap back to decency and the rule of law.”
In a second lawsuit obtained by Us on Thursday, Ganger and Renee’s partner, Rebecca Good, name Ross as well as several federal officials, including former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem. Renee’s family accuses officials of “targeting” the civil rights of Somali and Hispanic people through the immigration sweeps.
The docs claim that Rebecca has suffered severe emotional distress in the wake of Renee’s death. Furthermore, she mentioned being diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder after the grim discovery of finding “her partner bleeding from a gunshot wound to the head.”
“The complaints explain how the Administration created an environment during Operation Metro Surge in which federal agents believed they would be immune from consequences for violating those rules. There is no such immunity,” Good’s family attorney Antonio Romanucci said in a statement. “Renee’s death was not an accident. It was the predictable result of a coordinated campaign by senior officials in this administration to target Minnesotans of Somali or Hispanic origin and silence anyone who dared to raise their voice in protest.”
Trump, 80, and Noem, 54, previously defended Ross’ actions and claimed Renee was an agitator who tried to run over the officer with her vehicle.
The shooting, which was captured on cellphone video, triggered massive protests throughout the country and significant pushback from state leaders.

sources.news_title: The family of Renee Good files lawsuits over her death during Minneapolis ICE raids
sources.text:
The family of Renee Good, the 37-year-old killed last January by a federal agent during the Trump administration's immigration enforcement surge in Minnesota, filed two civil lawsuits against the federal government Thursday.
One of the lawsuits, against the United States government itself, is essentially a wrongful death case, arguing that Jonathan Ross, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who killed Good, violated his agency's own policies and the Fourth Amendment by using excessive force.
It is seeking damages for Good's family for the suffering she experienced in the final moments of her life. And also for her partner, Becca Good, who witnessed the killing. The lawsuit says she has suffered intense emotional distress from what she has experienced. Ross shot Renee Good several times in her car. At the time, federal officials claimed she had weaponized her vehicle, though video evidence contradicted that.
The other lawsuit is rarer, alleging that federal officials engaged in a conspiracy to interfere with the civil rights of people in Minnesota.
It argues that Good's death was the "predictable and intended product" of the immigration crackdown in the state and that Ross' actions were in furtherance of a "carefully planned, coordinated effort" to make Somali and Hispanic people the "object of aggression and abduction" and to silence the people "who observed, documented, and warned of that campaign."
In making that argument, the lawyers, with the firm Romanucci & Blandin, relied on the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871, which was used to combat the terrorism wrought by the KKK during the Reconstruction era.
"I would say the second lawsuit is very unusual," Rachel Moran, a law professor at the University of St. Thomas, told NPR. "It was immediately striking to me because the Trump administration has been aggressively using conspiracy charges, including here in Minnesota, against people involved in protesting the administration's immigration tactics."
Moran said the lawyers in the Good lawsuits seem to be "turning that tactic on its head" by arguing that administration officials are involved in an illegal conspiracy themselves.
According to Ben Berkman, one of the lawyers representing Good's family, the first lawsuit is about what federal officers did to Renee Good on a Minneapolis street last winter. The second is about why those officers were on that street in the first place.
"It reaches the agent who fired those shots at Renee and it reaches every official who put him on the street that day," Berkman said. "No mask, no badge and no title in the administration puts anyone above that law."
Those federal officials include Ross, but also White House adviser Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House Border czar Tom Homan, and former Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino, among others. NPR reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment, but did not hear back.
In a statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said, "We intend to vigorously defend these baseless civil lawsuits."
The lawsuit also lists 10 federal agents who were also present at the scene as John Does, noting that the federal government has not released their identities and that they were wearing masks at the time of the killing.
The civil charges also underscore a lack of criminal charges. DHS has provided little public indication that it is investigating Good's death or the death of Alex Pretti at the hands of Border Patrol agents a few weeks later in Minneapolis. According to The Trace, a news site that focuses on gun violence, nine people have been killed by immigration agents since President Trump took office again last year.
At the state level in Minnesota, local officials have also not filed charges or released the findings of any investigation. In a statement, a spokesperson for Hennepin County, where Minneapolis is located, told NPR that state and local officials are reviewing the evidence and that they will "communicate transparently when a decision is reached."
At the press conference held Thursday, Good's family seemed frustrated at the inaction on all levels. Civil suits, like the ones filed by the family today, have the potential to hold entire institutions accountable rather than just individual actors.
"The fact that there's been no accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy is completely mind-blowing," Brent Ganger, Good's brother, said. "We will not wait any longer. The time is absolutely now for accountability, for the deep damage done by ICE and others. We will not be quiet. We will not go away."
Brent and his mother, Donna Ganger, also testified before Congress last week at a hearing about fatal shootings by federal immigration officers.
In her first public appearance since the killing, Becca Good, Renee Good's partner, also spoke. She focused her words on who Renee was to her, calling her kind and loving, but also on what she has lost. Renee Good had three children, and Becca is still raising their youngest, a 6-year-old.
"This past August, I got ready to put our son in first grade. I bought him new shoes and a backpack and notebooks, pencil case, the whole nine yards. I went to Back To School Night on my own," Becca Good said. "She never missed a single moment. And this Halloween, it's our son's absolute favorite holiday. I'll take him trick or treating, without her hand in mine."

MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Renee Good’s family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials Thursday, alleging wrongful death, conspiracy and other violations in the 37-year-old woman’s killing by an immigration officer during a federal crackdown in Minneapolis.
The two lawsuits were filed by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and Renee’s brother Brent Ganger.
The Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to an email seeking comment.
Officer shot Good as she turned her car away from him
Renee Good was fatally shot Jan. 7 as protests against immigration raids flared across the city. According to Becca Good, her partner stopped their car in a street to support neighbors during an immigration operation.
Bystander video shows Renee Good in the driver’s seat of a red SUV blocking part of the road and repeatedly honking her horn.
Two immigration officers get out of a truck, their faces covered, and one orders Good to get out of the car. She reverses briefly, then turns the steering wheel as the officer says again, “get out of the car.”

Almost simultaneously, Becca Good, standing in the street, shouts: “Drive, baby, drive!”
One officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and fires into the windshield. He lurches back as the car turns away from him. The officer, who is now very close to the open window on the driver’s side, fires two more times, fatally shooting Renee Good, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.
Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense and that Good had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism.”
One lawsuit alleges wrongful death
The lawsuit against the United States of America seeks damages for Good’s wrongful death and “the immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family,” according to a news release by lawyers for Ganger and Good.
The lawsuit, which seeks a bench trial, also alleges “intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligent infliction of emotional distress” on Becca Good.
Becca and Renee Good, the mother of three children, were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives. They had only recently relocated to Minneapolis from Kansas City, Missouri.
Another lawsuit alleges conspiracy to conceal evidence
The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights and seeks a jury trial. It says the federal government moved to hide the evidence of what actually happened on Jan. 7.
The lawsuit says the shots fired by Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who killed Good, “were the predictable and intended product of the operation.”
It describes a “carefully planned, coordinated effort between senior federal officials and private actors to make two ethnic communities — Minnesotans of Somali and Hispanic descent and origin — the object of aggression and abduction, and to silence by intimidation, arrest and violence the neighbors and allies of those targeted communities who observed, documented and warned of that campaign.”
The lawsuit names Ross as a defendant, as well as: White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller; former Homeland Security head Kristi Noem; Corey Lewandowski, a campaign manager for President Donald Trump who also served as one of Noem’s advisers; White House border czar Tom Homan; former acting director of U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement Todd Lyons; former U.S. Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino; and 10 unnamed federal agents.
Good’s partner acknowledges other lives lost in immigration crackdown
The killing of Good and another U.S. citizen, Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis just weeks later sparked outrage across the country and calls to rein in immigration enforcement. At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration officers during President Donald Trump’s second term.
In social media accounts, Renee Good described herself as a “poet and writer and wife and mom.” On Pinterest, a profile picture shows her smiling and holding a young child, alongside posts about tattoos, hairstyles and home decorating.
In an interview shortly after her death, Renee Good’s mother, Donna Ganger, told The Associated Press: “She had this way of making you feel special and loved that I didn’t even understand that until we lost her.”
Good’s partner noted the broader loss to communities nationwide.
“As we have tried to navigate our own massive loss, I am also devastated by how many other lives have been destroyed in this darkest of times,” Becca Good said in the news release Thursday. “So many other families are dealing with the loss of their loved ones; to everyone who has had to witness it — the pain of this moment extends far beyond our family. What happened to us should never happen to any family.”

The filings include a wrongful death lawsuit and a complaint alleging a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights by senior federal officials, federal immigration enforcement agents, and private actors.
Renee Good’s killing came during an immigration enforcement effort led by ICE and Border Patrol agents in Minneapolis known as “Operation Metro Surge.”
Video of the shooting captured by agent Jonathan Ross showed him in front of the vehicle driven by Renee Good, who had stopped her burgundy SUV perpendicular to the street, obstructing the flow of traffic. Ross does not say anything as he walks across the front of the car toward the driver’s side of the car.
As he rounds the car, Renee Good can be seen with her window down looking directly at the officer. In the video, she then talks to Ross.
“That’s fine dude. I’m not mad at you,” she says. Ross does not respond. In the car window a reflection can be seen of Ross, holding his phone up, as he continues to walk. You can also hear the victim’s wife, Becca Good, say “show your face” to Ross.

She holds a cellphone up to Ross’ face as she addresses Ross.
“You wanna come at us? You wanna come at us? I say go get yourself some lunch, big boy,” Becca Good says to Ross. She then tries to get back in the car, but the door is locked.
You then hear another officer tell Renee Good, the driver, to “get out of the fucking car.”
She is then seen reversing the car and glancing forward as she turns the steering wheel to the right, away from where the officer is standing. The car moves forward, and Ross cries out “whoa” and then three gunshots are heard in rapid succession.

The lawsuit alleges “Operation Metro Surge” resulted in two dead Americans, a third person shot and more than $200 million in economic damage to a single city.
“Renee was one (of) those casualties,” the lawsuit states. “She was killed on a public street, while doing what thousands of her neighbors were doing that winter: watching masked, armed men terrorizing her community and refusing to look away.”

Family of Minneapolis woman killed by ICE agent files two federal lawsuits
One suit names the agent who fired the shots; the other names federal officials and alleges a broader civil rights violation
MINNEAPOLIS, Minn. (Valley News Live) - The family of a Minneapolis woman shot and killed by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in January has filed two federal lawsuits, accusing the agent and several federal officials of wrongdoing in her death.
Renee Nicole Macklin Good, 37, was shot three times by ICE agent Jonathan Ross on the morning of Jan. 7 on Portland Avenue in south Minneapolis, according to the lawsuits. Good had dropped her 6-year-old son off at school and was driving home through a neighborhood where federal agents were carrying out an immigration enforcement operation known as “Operation Metro Surge.”
According to the lawsuits, Good stopped her car in the street and honked her horn to alert neighbors to the agents’ presence. Her partner, Rebecca Good, got out to record the agents while Renee remained behind the wheel. Several vehicles, including Ross’s unmarked SUV, drove around her stopped car without incident.
The lawsuits allege that after agents ordered Good out of her car and one of them tried to open her door, she began slowly turning the wheel and driving away. Ross, who was no longer in the vehicle’s path, then drew his weapon and fired three rounds, the suits allege, striking Good’s forearm, her chest and, fatally, her left temple. No agent rendered aid, according to the lawsuits, and one agent turned away a bystander who identified himself as a physician and offered to help.
The Hennepin County Medical Examiner ruled Good’s death a homicide caused by multiple gunshot wounds, noting she was shot by a law enforcement officer, according to the complaints.
One lawsuit, filed under the Federal Tort Claims Act, names the United States as the defendant and alleges wrongful death, battery, assault, false imprisonment and negligence, claiming Ross’s actions violated the Fourth Amendment and the Department of Homeland Security’s own deadly force policy.
A second lawsuit names Ross and six federal officials individually, including former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House aide Stephen Miller and border czar Thomas Homan, alleging a civil rights conspiracy to target Minnesota’s Somali and Hispanic communities through the enforcement operation. That suit references a ruling in a separate federal case that found evidence immigration agents had stopped people based on ethnicity without reasonable suspicion.
Both lawsuits were filed Thursday by attorneys Kevin Riach and Antonio Romanucci on behalf of Good’s brother, acting as trustee for her next of kin, and Rebecca Good.
Good was a mother of three, served on her son’s school board and had no criminal history, according to the lawsuits. Rebecca Good says she has since been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder.
ICE and the Department of Homeland Security have not yet responded publicly to the lawsuits.
These are allegations contained in civil complaints. The claims have not been proven in court.

Renee Good’s family sues US government, immigration officials over her killing
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Renee Good’s family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials Thursday, alleging wrongful death and other violations of federal law in the 37-year-old woman’s killing by an immigration officer during a federal crackdown in Minneapolis.
The two lawsuits were filed by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and Renee’s brother Brent Ganger.
One lawsuit, filed against “the United States of America,” alleges the wrongful death of Renee Good under Minnesota law predicated on claims of battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence that caused her death.
The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights. It names as defendants: Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who shot her; White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller; former Homeland Security head Kristi Noem; former U.S. Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino, Corey Lewandowski, President Donald Trump’s campaign manager, and others.
Renee Good, a mother of three, was fatally shot Jan. 7 as protests against immigration raids flared across the city. According to Becca Good, her partner stopped their car in a street to support neighbors during an immigration operation.
Bystander video shows Renee Good in the driver’s seat of a red SUV blocking part of the road and repeatedly honking her horn.
Two immigration officers get out of a truck, their faces covered, and one orders Good to get out of the car. She reverses briefly, then turns the steering wheel as the officer says again, “get out of the car.”
Almost simultaneously, Becca Good, standing in the street, shouts: “Drive, baby, drive!”
One officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and fires into the windshield. He lurches back as the car turns away from him. The officer, who is now very close to the open window on the driver’s side, opens fire two more times, fatally shooting Renee Good, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.
Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense and that Good had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism.”
The killing of Good and another U.S. citizen, Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis just weeks later sparked outrage across the country and calls to rein in immigration enforcement. At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration officers during President Donald Trump’s second term.
In July, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer with a history of violent behavior fatally shot a 25-year-old Colombian man, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, in his car in Biddeford, Maine. Durán Guerrero was not the target of an immigration enforcement action.
Last week, immigration enforcement agents shot and wounded a Venezuelan delivery driver in Austin, Texas. Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez, 28, survived but was charged with sideswiping an officer with his car mirror and later attempting to strike an officer with the vehicle.
Becca and Renee Good were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives. They had only recently relocated to Minneapolis from Kansas City, Missouri.
In social media accounts, Renee Good described herself as a “poet and writer and wife and mom.” On Pinterest, a profile picture shows her smiling and holding a young child, alongside posts about tattoos, hairstyles and home decorating.
In an interview shortly after her death, Renee Good’s mother, Donna Ganger, told The Associated Press: “She had this way of making you feel special and loved that I didn’t even understand that until we lost her.”

The new filings are the latest effort to sue the Trump administration over its sweeping immigration enforcement efforts, with the same law firm representing Good's family recently pursuing legal action against agents involved in the raids in Illinois under Operation Midway Blitz.
What the Family Alleges Happened
The lawsuit opens with a description of the events of January 7. It says Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, dropped her son at school, drove home through her neighborhood, and stopped her car in the middle of Portland Avenue, where federal agents were operating.
Good honked her car horn to warn her neighbors, the complaint said, and her partner got out of the vehicle and started to film while Good stayed behind the wheel.
While Renee Good was not the target of the operation, multiple unmarked vehicles stopped around her car, the complaint alleged, including one driven by ICE agent Jonathan Ross.
After passing Good, Ross allegedly got out of his car and circled her vehicle while filming, at which point Good spoke to him: "That’s fine dude. I’m not mad at you. I’m not mad at any of you," she was heard saying on video.
As other agents pulled up, she allegedly waved them around and told them to "just go around," but instead the agents told her to get out of the car.
The plaintiffs said Good turned her wheels away from Ross and began to move forward, at which point they allege that he stepped sideways before drawing his weapon and firing a shot at the bottom left of her windshield, the complaint said.
As Good turned her car in "its slow turn away from him," the filing said, Ross allegedly fired two more rounds through her open driver's side window, one of which hit her left temple.
"As her car careened out of control down Portland Avenue and crashed into a parked car, Ross cursed, 'fucking bitch,'" the complaint alleged, adding that no federal agent rendered aid to her and denied a doctor's attempt to reach her.
The complaint describes how Becca Good was beside the front passenger door when Ross allegedly fired his gun.
"She ran down the street after Renee’s car and found her partner bleeding from a gunshot wound to the head," the complaint read. "Becca has suffered immensely as a result of the unlawful shooting and killing of her partner, and she has been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder."
Why Miller, Homan, and Noem Are Being Sued
The lawsuit does not just target the federal agent accused of killing Good. It also lists Trump administration officials, including White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Border Czar Tom Homan, as defendants.
According to the complaint, Miller, a key architect of President Donald Trump's immigration policies across both terms, repeatedly defined the Minnesota operation as being about a specific ethnic group—those of Somali heritage, largely due to the alleged fraud under investigation in the state at the time.
The plaintiffs allege that Miller directed operations in the Twin Cities through daily calls with Noem and then-acting ICE Director Todd Lyons, telling them to dispatch agents to "force confrontations" with people observing and protesting the operation, such as Good.
Noem is accused of pushing policies at DHS that allowed the agents working the operation to keep their faces covered, and of carrying out enforcement in a way that could be a "filmed spectacle," the complaint said. The former secretary was also accused of embedding conservative social media influencers into field operations to document what was happening.
Homan was included in the lawsuit because he was "the public architect" of the sweeping citywide operations, the complaint said, with the filing quoting Homan promising to "flood the zone" when referring to sanctuary cities.
After Good, and later Alex Pretti, were fatally shot in Minneapolis, Homan was the public face of the efforts to ease tensions. He worked with local and state officials, eventually withdrawing hundreds of agents from the region.
Trump previously spoke on Good's death, saying in an interview with CBS News January 13, "I love all of our people... and I would bet you that she, under normal circumstances, was a very solid, wonderful person — but her actions were pretty tough.
"I’ve seen it many ways… the bottom line is we have hundreds of thousands of murderers in our country, killers, ICE is trying to get them out… their job is being made very difficult… when you look at the way that car was pulled away… there are a couple versions of that tape that are very very bad.”
Separate Lawsuit Against the US
The other lawsuit was filed under the Federal Tort Claims Act and lists only the U.S. as the defendant.
The 32-page filing removes the conspiracy allegations, instead focusing on seeking damages from the government for wrongful death, battery, false imprisonment, negligence and emotional distress.
FTCA filings are used to seek the prosecution of federal agents who are often granted immunity from lawsuits if their conduct is considered part of their official duties. The claim filed Thursday argues that Ross and other agents breached their official duties.
Speaking to reporters Thursday, attorney Antonio Romanucci said he was confident in the two complaints and their legal standing, adding that he would expect the judge who takes up the cases to be impartial, while Good's brother called for justice.
"I stand here with fierce determination to do what is right for my sister, for her children, and for our country—and that is to insist on accountability," Brent Ganger, Renee Good’s brother, said in a press release Thursday. "What happened to her on January 7th and what has happened to far too many people in the last year is not what America is about. We can and must do better, and the Constitution must be the road map back to decency and the rule of law."
Update 10/1/26, 3:12 p.m. ET: This article was updated with comment from the White House.

Renee Good's Family Sues Immigration Officials Over Her Killing in Minneapolis

By Kathy Mccormack and Mark Vancleave
MINNEAPOLIS — Renee Good’s family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials Thursday, alleging wrongful death, conspiracy and other violations in the 37-year-old woman’s killing by an immigration officer during a federal crackdown in Minneapolis.
The two lawsuits were filed by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and Renee’s brother Brent Ganger.
The Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to an email seeking comment on the lawsuits.
Trending
Renee Good, a mother of three, was fatally shot Jan. 7 as protests against immigration raids flared across the city. According to Becca Good, her partner stopped their car in a street to support neighbors during an immigration operation.
Bystander video shows Renee Good in the driver’s seat of a red SUV blocking part of the road and repeatedly honking her horn.
Two immigration officers get out of a truck, their faces covered, and one orders Good to get out of the car. She reverses briefly, then turns the steering wheel as the officer says again, “get out of the car.”
Almost simultaneously, Becca Good, standing in the street, shouts: “Drive, baby, drive!”
One officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and fires into the windshield. He lurches back as the car turns away from him. The officer, who is now very close to the open window on the driver’s side, opens fire two more times, fatally shooting Renee Good, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.
Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense and that Good had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism.”
The lawsuit against the United States of America seeks damages for Good’s wrongful death and “the immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family,” according to a news release filed by lawyers for Ganger and Good.
The lawsuit also alleges “intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligent infliction of emotional distress” on Becca Good.
Becca and Renee Good were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives. They had only recently relocated to Minneapolis from Kansas City, Missouri. It asks for a bench trial.
The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights and seeks a jury trial.
It says the shots fired by Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who killed Good, “were the predictable and intended product of the operation,” which the lawsuit describes as a “carefully planned, coordinated effort between senior federal officials and private actors to make two ethnic communities — Minnesotans of Somali and Hispanic descent and origin — the object of aggression and abduction, and to silence by intimidation, arrest and violence the neighbors and allies of those targeted communities who observed, documented and warned of that campaign,” according to the news release.
The lawsuit also alleges “collaboration of federal agencies and individuals with private entities for an operation with discriminatory design, racially targeted pursuit and seizure of individuals without regard to their legal status, and each defendant’s participation in the conspiracy.”
It names Ross as a defendant, as well as: White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller; former Homeland Security head Kristi Noem; former U.S. Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino; Corey Lewandowski, President Donald Trump’s campaign manager, and others.
The killing of Good and another U.S. citizen, Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis just weeks later sparked outrage across the country and calls to rein in immigration enforcement. At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration officers during President Donald Trump’s second term.
In social media accounts, Renee Good described herself as a “poet and writer and wife and mom.” On Pinterest, a profile picture shows her smiling and holding a young child, alongside posts about tattoos, hairstyles and home decorating.
In an interview shortly after her death, Renee Good’s mother, Donna Ganger, told The Associated Press: “She had this way of making you feel special and loved that I didn’t even understand that until we lost her.”
“As we have tried to navigate our own massive loss, I am also devastated by how many other lives have been destroyed in this darkest of times,” Becca Good said in the news release Thursday. “So many other families are dealing with the loss of their loved ones; to everyone who has had to witness it — the pain of this moment extends far beyond our family. What happened to us should never happen to any family.”
McCormack reported from Concord, New Hampshire.

Family of Renee Good sues US government and Trump officials over her death
By Whitney Wild, Rebekah Riess, CNN
(CNN) — The family of an American woman shot and killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent has filed two civil lawsuits related to her death, according to court records filed Thursday in Minnesota federal court.
Renee Good was killed January 7 by ICE agent Jonathan Ross in Minneapolis during the height of the Department of Homeland Security’s Operation Metro Surge, prompting significant protest in the city and sparking national outrage.
“The hole in my family and myself, created by my sister’s passing, is hauntingly apparent,” Good’s brother and plaintiff, Brent Ganger, said at a Thursday news conference announcing the lawsuits.
“Since Renee’s death, no meaningful change has occurred. The deaths of innocent Americans by taxpayer-funded government agents should not be a partisan issue, and it should alarm every American.”
One lawsuit names the United States of America as the sole defendant under the Federal Tort Claims Act, a federal law that allows people to sue the US government for personal injury, property damage or death, caused by alleged negligence of federal employees acting within their job duties.
The lawsuit seeks unspecified compensatory damages for Good’s partner, who witnessed the shooting, and “for the immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family,” the family’s attorneys said in a statement.
In January, attorneys sent letters to the federal agencies connected with Good’s death, notifying them of their intention to pursue legal action. Under FTCA guidelines, they waited six months for a response, which could be a denial, agreement to payment, or simply a non-response, attorney Sarah Raisch said.
“We are here today because we have not heard from the government, either that they will accept the claim, or not,” attorney Antonio Romanucci said.
A tort lawsuit against the federal government, from guilt or innocence to the amount of a potential award, is typically decided by a federal judge.
In their second lawsuit, Good’s family alleges, among other things, Operation Metro Surge was “a carefully planned, coordinated effort between senior federal officials and private actors” to interfere with the civil rights of Minnesotans of Somali and Hispanic descent and origin, and to silence “the neighbors and allies of those targeted communities who observed, documented, and warned of that campaign.”
The suit names Ross, ten John Doe federal agents, and several current and former Trump administration officials as defendants, including White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, White House border czar Tom Homan, former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem, and Greg Bovino, the former Border Patrol official who led the administration’s immigration enforcement surge in Minneapolis.
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said the Trump administration intends “to vigorously defend these baseless civil lawsuits.”
Bis also pointed to President Donald Trump’s remarks to CBS News about Good from January, in which he said “I love all of our people … and I would bet you that she, under normal circumstances, was a very solid, wonderful person. But, you know, her actions were pretty tough.” Trump also defended ICE, saying the job of federal agents was “being made very difficult.”
CNN has reached out to DHS, and phone numbers listed under Noem’s name for comment. Bovino declined to comment about the lawsuit.
The lawsuit alleges the shots fired by Ross were “the predictable and intended product of the operation,” according to the family’s attorneys.
The lawsuit seeks unspecified compensatory and punitive damages.
‘Like trying to live without the sun’
Good’s partner and plaintiff, Becca Good, spoke publicly for the first time since the deadly shooting took place. During the Thursday news conference, she called Good “the center” of her universe and spoke about taking their 6-year-old son to first grade without her.
“Living without her is like trying to live without the sun. And you don’t know how much light something gives you until it’s gone, and then you feel that absence every single second,” she said, becoming emotional.
Renee Good loved her three children, her partner said, and enjoyed reading them books, and talking about music and comics with them.
“Every morning, she is my first thought. I think about how the kids are growing up without their mama, and how I’ll grow old without the love of my life,” she said. “But I also think a lot about what she would have wanted after all of this.”
Becca Good said the family is pursuing legal action because “Renee’s love and legacy demand a better world for her children, for this community, and for this country.”
“What happened to us should never happen to any family,” Good said. “Accountability and change — true accountability — is the only way to make sure that no other family has to go through what we have.”
“I don’t hate the people who took Renee from us, but what I want them to understand is – every single day, they get to look at their children, and their wives, and their sisters, and know what they took from our family,” Good said. “They took a mother away from her children. They know that, and they will carry it forever.”
How the deadly shooting unfolded in Minneapolis
Good, a mother of three, had just finished dropping her 6-year-old son off at school when she encountered ICE agents.
The moments leading up to the shooting were captured by bystanders as well as Ross, a 10-year ICE veteran, whose cellphone video starts with him in front of Good’s burgundy SUV. The vehicle was stopped for a few minutes perpendicular to a snowy residential Minneapolis street, obstructing the flow of traffic.
Ross did not say anything as he walked from the front of the car toward the driver’s side.
Good then addressed Ross, the video shows.
“That’s fine, dude. I’m not mad at you,” she says. Ross didn’t respond.
Becca Good was standing outside the car and said “show your face” to Ross, whose masked reflection is seen on the vehicle’s windows as he continues walking around it. Becca Good holds her cellphone up, seemingly recording Ross, and tells him, “You wanna come at us? You wanna come at us? I say go get yourself some lunch, big boy.”
She then tries to get back into the car, but the door is locked.
Another officer then tells Renee Good to “get out of the f**king car.”
Renee Good is then seen reversing the car and glancing forward as she turns the steering wheel to the right. The car moves forward, Ross cries out, “whoa,” and three gunshots are heard. Good was shot shortly after 9:30 a.m., according to a news release from the city government.
The video filmed by Ross captured audio of gunshots but doesn’t show the actual moment of the shooting, though other video from bystanders shows Ross was standing out of the vehicle’s path when he opened fire. He fired first into her windshield and then at close range through the open driver’s side window, videos show.
The end of Ross’s video shows the SUV as it barrels forward. Someone can be heard saying, “f**king b*tch.”
DHS later said Good “weaponized her vehicle” to run over an officer near an ICE vehicle.
The search for accountability for the shooting remains ongoing. In March, the Hennepin County Attorney’s Office and two state agencies sued the Trump administration for access to evidence in Good’s shooting death as well as the death of Alex Pretti, who was killed by DHS agents in January.
In July, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced the Department of Justice had provided a trove of materials related to both shootings to state investigators. No charges have been filed in either case.
This story has been updated with additional information.

“And this Halloween, our son’s absolute favorite holiday, I’ll take him trick-or-treating without her hand in mine,” she said. “Every single one of these moments, for all of her babies and for everyone up here, was a monument moment and she should be here for all of them.”

“She was the center of my universe, and living without her is like trying to live without the sun,” she said. “And you don’t know how much light something gives you until it’s gone, and then you feel that absence every single second.”
Becca and Good’s parents and four siblings appeared alongside their attorneys Thursday at the University of St. Thomas to announce the filing of two lawsuits against the federal government and immigration agents.
The suits allege that the government caused Good’s wrongful death, and conspired to violate her civil rights. The family’s attorneys did not specify how much they’re seeking in damages. Becca said the suits “are taking steps to build a world Renee would have wanted.”
Good’s family cried as Becca tearfully said Good is “her first thought” every morning, and that watching their son grow up without her is the “hardest thing I’ve ever had to do.” Good’s mother Donna Ganger, caressed Becca’s arm as she spoke at a podium during the family’s news conference.
“I think about how we should’ve had forty, sixty more years together, but I also think about what she would’ve wanted out of all of this,” Becca said.
She said she doesn’t “hate the people who took Renee from us,” but hopes they understand the impact losing Good has had on her family, and that they carry that “forever.”
Becca described Good as a doting mother who read to her three children and shared music and comics with them. Good has two children from first marriage and a third child from her second marriage.
“She gave them all the room and the encouragement and the safety to grow into their own people,” Becca said. “She nurtured every one of their interests.”
The pain of losing Good was underscored this year, Becca said, when she went back-to-school shopping in August to prepare their son for first grade.
“I bought him new shoes and a backpack and notebooks, pencil case – whole nine yards – and I went to back-to-school night on my own,” she said. “[Renee] never missed a single moment.”
She thanked Minneapolis residents for their support in the wake of Good’s killing, and said they chose to live here because the community is “unlike anything we experienced in all the places we both have lived.”
“It was exactly what we’ve both been searching for for so long – our home,” she said. “And I really could never say enough about the love and support that this community gave to me and countless others since that day.”
Residents have offered meals, rides and babysitting help.
Brent Ganger, Good’s brother, said while his parents are “lifelong” Republican voters, he’s a moderate and other relatives lean more Democrat. Yet their family “love each other” despite the political differences, he added.
“Our family proves that even in the darkest of times, we can and should stay together,” he said.
He said he “deeply regrets” that it took Good’s death to realize that no one is “untouchable.”
“It has taken far too long for white people like me to know what it feels like to not feel safe in this country,” he said. “My brothers and sisters of color have always had a hard time feeling safe from police, and many for good reason, still don’t.”
Good’s brother and Becca said they want accountability for Renee, and to protect other families.
“Today we are taking steps to build the world Renee would have wanted,” Becca said. “The world I promised our son every night when I tuck him in — this is the world that she believed in. It’s the world I’m gonna fight for, and it’s the world I’m going to raise our son in.”
Becca and Good’s family did not address questions after their remarks.
Good, 37, a Minneapolis resident and mother of three, was killed at 34th Street and Portland Avenue in south Minneapolis while observing immigration enforcement activity during Operation Metro Surge.
“The world was stunned by what they saw on January 7,” said Antonio Romanucci, lead attorney on the two lawsuits. “Our government normalized and neutralized what our eyes saw.”
Romanucci presented images at the news conference showing screenshots from a video that captured the shooting. One image showed Jonathan Ross, the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent who shot Good, standing in front of her vehicle.
“He willingly, knowingly placed himself in front of Renee’s vehicle,” Romanucci said.
Another image showed Ross near Good on the driver’s side of the vehicle after he had fired the first shot.
“No one, including Ross, was in the path of the vehicle at that point,” Romanucci said, “and he fired the second shot or the third shot.”
What the lawsuits allege
One suit filed against the United States of America alleges that the government caused Good’s wrongful death under a Minnesota statute predicated on battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and negligence.
The lawsuit is filed under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows individuals to sue the U.S. government in federal court for personal injury, death or property damage.
It says that Ganger brings this suit “to recover for the immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life”; and from Becca “to recover for the severe emotional distress, and its attendant physical manifestations, that the agents’ conduct has inflicted upon her.”
The lawsuit also details the events that led to her fatal shooting that morning and claims that the agents’ action violated the Fourth Amendment and U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s own policies.
Another lawsuit was filed against Ross, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, former Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, political operative Corey Lewandowski, border czar Tom Homan, former acting ICE director Todd Lyons, former Border Patrol leader Gregory Bovino, and ten other federal agents identified as “John Doe.”
It alleges several counts, including conspiracy to deprive Somali Hispanic residents equal protections under the law. The suit accuses Ross of using excessive force. It lists several claims under Minnesota tort law, including wrongful death, battery, assault and false imprisonment.
Case history
The Hennepin County Attorney’s Office and Minnesota Attorney General’s Office are investigating Good’s killing, but no criminal charges have been filed in state or federal court against the immigration agent who shot Good.
Good’s mother, Donna Ganger, testified in front of Congress last week with family members of other victims killed by federal immigration agents. Stella Carlson, a bystander who filmed the Jan. 24 killing of Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, also testified.
“We need action. We need accountability. We need this never ever to happen again and destroy another family or a community,” Ganger testified.
Good’s older brother, Brent Granger, also testified.
“In the days since my sister’s death, ICE agents have continued to intimidate, assault, hurt, and kill innocent people,” he testified. “Since Renee’s death, no meaningful changes occurred.”
Attorneys representing Good’s family are conducting a civil investigation into the shooting, and filed a motion in April to retrieve the Honda Pilot she was driving when she was killed.
Taking legal action against the federal government is a long, complex process, and “always challenging” because state and local law enforcement officers have “many immunities,” according to a Jan. 14 statement from Antonio Romanucci, one of Good’s attorneys.
“This process will not deter us in any way from fervently pursuing justice on behalf of Renee Good,” said Romanucci’s Jan. 14 statement.
According to the motion to recover Good’s vehicle: Good and Becca dropped off their 6-year-old son at school on Jan. 7 and were driving home when they stopped to observe federal agents in their neighborhood. Good stayed in the driver’s seat as Becca exited the vehicle to film the agents. As bystanders recorded videos at the scene, Good motioned for other vehicles to pass her vehicle, which was parked in the middle of the street.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent Jonathan Ross exited his vehicle and started filming with his phone. He walked in front of Good’s vehicle as she started to turn her vehicle to the right away from Ross and slowly moved forward, according to the motion.
“Ross was at no point in danger from the vehicle,” read the motion. “Notwithstanding the absence of any threat, Ross drew his gun and fired at least three times at Renee.”
Then-U.S. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem called Good a “domestic terrorist,” and blamed Gov. Tim Walz and Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey for refusing to cooperate with federal officials on immigration enforcement.
Becca described Good as someone who showed up for others as a “volunteer, a mom, a friend” in a Feb. 7 statement released by her attorneys.
“Renee was not the first person killed, and she was not the last,” Becca’s February statement said. “You know my wife’s name and you know Alex’s name, but there are many others in this city being harmed that you don’t know — their families are hurting just like mine, even if they don’t look like mine. They are neighbors, friends, coworkers, classmates. And we must also know their names. Because this shouldn’t happen to anyone.”
Other ICE fatalities, injuries
At least 58 people have died in ICE custody and at least 20 people have been shot since the start of the second Trump administration, according to lawmakers at last week’s congressional hearing. Two other Minneapolis residents were killed during Operation Metro Surge.
Julio Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan man, was shot and wounded in the leg by ICE agent Christian Castro on Jan. 14 in North Minneapolis. Sosa-Celis and his roommate, Alfredo Aljorna, were charged and taken into federal custody. City surveillance video that captured the shooting contradicted Castro’s claims that he was attacked by Sosa-Celis, Aljorna and a third man with a broom and shovel. The federal charges against Sosa-Celis and Ajlorna were dismissed.
The U.S. Department of Justice charged Castro in May with allegedly lying about the shooting. The Hennepin County Attorney’s Office charged Castro on May 18 with four counts of second-degree assault using a dangerous weapon and one count of falsely reporting a crime in the shooting.
Alex Pretti, an intensive care nurse, was shot and killed by multiple federal agents on Jan. 24 on Nicollet Avenue. Videos that captured the shooting showed that agents tackled Pretti to the ground and shot him after he tried to help a woman who had been pushed down by an agent.
The Hennepin County Attorney and Minnesota Attorney General’s offices are investigating all three shootings, and filed a lawsuit in mid-March against the federal government for refusing to release evidence in the cases. Federal officials agreed six months later to release some evidence to local officials.
Sahan staff writers Shubhanjana Das and Katrina Pross, and digital producer Alberto Villafan contributed to this report.

The family of Renee Good, the mother shot and killed by an ICE agent in Minnesota this year, has filed two federal lawsuits alleging wrongful death.
Good, 37, was fatally shot on January 7 on Portland Avenue in Minneapolis after a confrontation with ICE agent Jonathan Ross, who opened fire on her as she sat behind the wheel of her Honda Pilot SUV, apparently attempting to leave the scene of their argument.
“Renee’s death was not an accident,” the law firm representing Good’s family, Romanucci and Blandin, said in a statement.
“It was the predictable result of a coordinated campaign by senior officials in this administration to target Minnesotans of Somali or Hispanic origin and silence anyone who dared to raise their voice in protest.”
Attacking the federal immigration crackdown where the agent was deployed, they said: “Operation Metro Surge was built on exaggerated fraud accusations that the White House embraced as a pretext for thousands of masked, unidentified federal agents to rove neighborhoods and stop people based on how they looked.
“Administration officials told agents to force confrontations with observers like Renee and led agents to believe they would face no consequences for using force.”
The two lawsuits were filed by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and the deceased’s brother Brent Ganger.
The first, filed against “the United States of America,” alleges the wrongful death of Renee Nicole Macklin Good under Minnesota law predicated on claims of battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence that caused her death.
The second alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights. It names among the defendants: Ross, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller; former Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem; former Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino, Corey Lewandowski and “John Doe federal agents 1-10.”
Good’s death was met with a huge public outcry, not least because it was seen around the world in viral cell footage recorded by several bystanders.
The protests only grew louder when another citizen, intensive care nurse Alex Pretti, was also killed by federal agents in the same city later that month, prompting locals to take to the streets amid the bitter winter cold to protest against the incursion.
Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey told ICE to “get the f*** out” of the city and Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison said the agents has sown chaos and terror across the metropolitan area.”
In the footage of Good’s final moments, she was seen in the driver’s seat of her vehicle blocking part of the road and repeatedly honking her horn to draw attention to the presence of the agents.
Two immigration officers got out of a truck, their faces covered, before one ordered Good to get out of her car. She reversed briefly, then turned the steering wheel as the officer said again: “Get out of the car.”
“Drive, baby, drive!” Becca Good can be heard urging from the sidewalk.
An officer, later identified as Ross, then drew his weapon and fired into the SUV’s windshield. He lurched back as the car turned away from him.
The officer, who was very close to the open window on the driver’s side, fired twice more, fatally shooting Good.
She was taken to Hennepin County Medical Center, with emergency responders attempting to resuscitate her en route, only to be pronounced dead.
Federal officials reacted at the time by insisting the officer had acted in self-defense and that the deceased had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism,” a claim that was widely dismissed and ultimately played a part in Noem’s eventual downfall and demotion but was nevertheless also endorsed by President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance.
The secretary was later dismissed from the DHS by the president and made “Special Envoy to the Shield of the Americas, She was replaced by former Oklahoma Sen. Markwayne Mullin.
Good, who had only recently moved to Minneapolis when she died, was remembered by her mother, Donna Granger, as “extremely compassionate” and not the type of person to confront ICE agents.
“Renee was one of the kindest people I’ve ever known,” she told The Minneapolis Star Tribune of her late daughter. “She was extremely compassionate. She’s taken care of people all her life. She was loving, forgiving and affectionate. She was an amazing human being.”
The killings of Good and Pretti account for two of the 10 people known to have died in encounters with immigration officers during Trump’s second term.
In July, an ICE officer fatally shot a 25-year-old Colombian man, Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero, in his car in Biddeford, Maine. Last week, immigration agents shot and wounded Venezuelan delivery driver Rafael Garces-Perez, 28, in Austin, Texas.

MINNEAPOLIS — Nearly nine months after Renee Good was fatally shot by a federal agent, her family has announced two civil lawsuits.
"The day of accountability has arrived," Antonio Romanucci, one of the attorneys for the family, said during a news conference Thursday morning in Minneapolis.
ADVERTISEMENT
The law firms Romanucci & Blandin and Riach Law, representing the family of Renee Good, filed the suits Thursday, Oct. 1, against the United States, federal agents and federal officials for Good's Jan. 7 death in Minneapolis during the height of Operation Metro Surge.
“ICE and CBP are not above the Constitution,” Romanucci said. “Federal agents do not get a free pass to use excessive force against ordinary people exercising their rights — rights that are available to all people, not some people or a segregated class of people.”
Renee's partner, Becca Good, made her first public comments since January at Thursday's news conference announcing the lawsuits.
"I don't hate the people who took Renee from us, but I want them to understand every single day they get to look at their children, their wives and their sisters, and know what they took from our family. They took a mother away from her children. They know that, and they will carry it forever," Becca Good said.
Renee’s brother, Brent Ganger, also spoke Thursday. He and their mother, Donna Ganger, recently testified at a congressional hearing on Sept. 22.
“Our family has waited. Our country has waited, and we will not wait any longer. The time is absolutely now for accountability,” Brent said. “We will not be quiet. We will not go away. We filed these two lawsuits today to put officials on notice that we have not forgotten.”
Brent said that since his sister’s death, there has been “no meaningful change.”
ADVERTISEMENT
“We do not want her used as a political pawn, but rather as an agent for peace for all. In the days since my sister's death, ICE agents have continued to intimidate, assault, hurt, and kill innocent people,” he said.
Brent said his family has a mix of political beliefs: his parents are lifelong Republican voters, he is a moderate, and others are left-leaning.
“Our family proves that even in the darkest of times, we can and should stay united,” he said. “We expect nothing less from our fellow Americans, and especially leaders in this country and Congress.”
The lawsuits allege that Jonathan Ross, the man identified as the federal agent who shot Renee Good, as well as other agents on the scene, violated several of the Department of Homeland Security's own policies.
Some of those policies listed include the department's use-of-force policies and the requirement that agents obtain medical assistance for injured parties as soon as possible.
In one example, the complaint details when a bystander wanted to help Renee Good after the shooting and said they were a physician, and an unnamed agent allegedly responded: “I don’t care.”
Lawyers are also arguing in the legal action that Renee’s death was not an accident, that it was the “predictable result of a coordinated campaign” by the federal administration to “target” Minnesotans of Somali or Hispanic descent and to “silence anyone who dared to raise their voice in protest.”
ADVERTISEMENT
“No one was armed, no one was a domestic terrorist,” Romanucci said of Renee and Becca. “Renee had the right to speak. She had the right to express herself. She had the right to assemble. She had the right to observe what Operation Metro Surge was doing.”
He said the “cover story” from federal officials in the immediate aftermath, which was that Ross was justified in his use of force, “would crumble once the video was played and the facts exposed.”
The attorneys spoke Thursday about how federal law enforcement can't be prosecuted the same as local law enforcement, which is part of why they filed two separate lawsuits — one against the U.S. under the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) and the other against federal agents and federal officials, under the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871.
The defendants in the second lawsuit are: Jonathan Ross, Stephen Miller, Kristi Noem, Corey R. Lewandowski, Thomas D. Homan, Todd Lyons, Gregory Bovino and unnamed Federal Agents 1-10.
The civil suits come after months without a decision on potential criminal charges from the Hennepin County Attorney's Office, the state, or federal prosecutors for the agents involved.
Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty has charged two other ICE agents for other, non-fatal incidents during Operation Metro Surge, but no agents involved in the Good or Alex Pretti fatal shootings.
Two-way evidence sharing with the federal government in those cases began in July — six months after their deaths.
ADVERTISEMENT
The last time Moriarty was asked about charging decisions, on Sept. 17, she repeated what she has said at previous press conferences: "We continue to investigate both of those cases." She has declined to give any kind of timeline on when a decision could come.
Romanucci said Thursday criminal charges are the "extreme hope," but wouldn't comment on discussions with government officials. He also emphasized the need for a "true investigation."
"There should be accountability at all levels here, and one of them being criminal," he said. "If a crime was committed, then it deserves to be investigated and prosecuted and let a jury decide, just like we have seen in this city before."
Becca Good said Renee's legacy demands a better world for her children, her community and her country. She said what happened to her family "should not happen to any family, regardless of who you are, who you voted for, or what you believe."
"Today we are taking a step to build the world Renee would have wanted — the one I promise our son I am working towards every night when I tuck him in," Becca said. "This is the world that she believed in. This is the world I'm going to fight for, and that's the world I'm going to raise our son in."
